name: Bilal Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Night, mostly. I drive an articulated lorry on trunk runs for a parcel carrier, from the hub outside town to a big sorting centre three hours up the motorway and back. Clock on at eight in the evening, hook up the trailer, and it's mostly motorway in the dark with a podcast on. The quiet is nice. What wears me out is the sleep, because I'm never quite on the same clock as anyone else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the cab?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a house with two mates near the station, so rent's cheap-ish, but I've still only got a couple of weeks of money saved. Pay's on the low side for artic work round here, and there aren't many other haulage firms nearby. I use AI every day, honestly. I've had it quiz me on electrics during my breaks, and it plans my weekend shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit disappointing, to be honest. I'd post something like, so much for the future, back to the motorway. Most of the lads would laugh at me for being let down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays, but it stays low paid with rubbish hours. Nights on the trunk route wreck your body, and there's no pay rise coming because the carrier's always squeezing the contract. I'd still be living month to month, just without the excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep doing the free electrics course I started online. I'd want to get a proper electrical qualification by evenings, so in five years I can get off nights. And I'd stay in the union because the pay fight still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, a bit bored, a bit stuck. Not scared, just restless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrics, if driving's not going anywhere in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my uncle drove trunk runs for twenty years and his back's gone. I don't want to be on nights at forty. Electrics is daytime work and pays better once you're qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the qualification with two weeks saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. The college does it in modules, so I'd pay one module at a time and skip the summer festival. My housemate Kyle says I'm mad, but he also says it every time I change my phone plan.

say: I'd post that it's **disappointing** and joke about going back to the motorway.
Most drivers would **laugh** at me for being let down.
think: The job stays but stays **low paid** with hard night hours.
I'd still be living **month to month**, with no pay rise coming.
do: Keep **driving** trunk runs while studying electrics at night.
Pay for an **electrical qualification** one college module at a time.
Stay in the **union** for the pay fight.
feel: **Restless** and a bit stuck, but **not scared**.
S0.quote: My uncle drove trunk runs for twenty years and his back's gone. I don't want to be on nights at forty.
fieldNote: Bilal is the rare driver who feels **let down** that nothing changes.
His plan to leave nights comes from his **uncle's back**, not from AI.
His thin savings shape the **pace** of his plans, not whether he makes them.

steps.text: Pay for an evening electrical qualification one module at a time
Keep driving the night trunk run to the sorting centre
Skip the summer festival to cover the next college module

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the carrier should share the savings and train us for whatever comes next. I'd post about it, and I'd tell the union rep we should get ahead of it instead of reacting. Some people would think I'm a traitor for liking the tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job is already small. The routes are planned for me and the paperwork's on the tablet, so software taking more of that barely touches my day. The driving still needs me in this picture. The bigger risk is the office using AI to cut trunk runs or merge loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI planning tools properly and learn how the carrier's new systems work, because the people who understand them get the day jobs. I'd ask about any trainee roles in fleet maintenance at the hub. And I'd keep plugging away at the electrics course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy. I think I'd be on the right side of it if I keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the hub would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planners in the hub office. There are four of them and most of what they do is exactly what the card says AI takes over. One of them, Gwen, has been there twenty years and hates computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some people would think you're a traitor. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say liking the tech isn't the same as liking the bosses. I want the tech and a union that makes sure we get our share. Those two things go together for me.

say: I'd say the carrier must **share savings** and fund retraining.
I'd urge the union to **get ahead** of the change, not react.
think: Planning and paperwork are a **small part** of my day already.
The real risk is the office **cutting or merging** trunk runs.
do: Learn the carrier's new **planning systems** properly.
Ask about **trainee roles** in fleet maintenance at the hub.
Keep going with the **electrics course** in the evenings.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit uneasy, confident if he **keeps moving**.
S1.quote: Liking the tech isn't the same as liking the bosses. I want the tech and a union that makes sure we get our share.
fieldNote: Bilal separates **technology** from who benefits from it, which is central to him.
He worries more for the **hub planners** than for himself.
His thinking work is small, so this picture touches him **lightly**.

steps.text: Learn the carrier's new route and load planning tools
Apply for a fleet maintenance trainee role at the hub
Push the union rep to bargain early over automation savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper public plan, with the gains taxed and shared. Motorway trunk runs are the easiest thing in the world to automate, so we'd be first. I'd be online every day making that case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's hub to hub, motorway, at night, no customers. My exact job is the first in line once the robots come in 2031. They'd probably start trials even before that. With two weeks of savings, I can't just quit and retrain full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard at the electrics, two evenings a week instead of one, and try to get onto the hub's maintenance team for the driverless trucks themselves. I'd ask the carrier for a transfer to day work so I can study. If the union gets a retraining fund, I'd be first in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but buzzing too, which sounds strange. It's frightening and fascinating at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the maintenance jobs go to people with more qualifications than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the real fear. There might be ten of those jobs for a hundred drivers. If I don't get one, I'd look at installing chargers for electric trucks, which is still electrics but out on sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots in 2031. What changes for you in that gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the gap the trucks still need me, but everyone around me is being replaced by software, so the carrier's hungry to cut. I'd use those three years like a countdown clock. Every month I'm not studying is a month wasted.

say: I'd demand a **public plan** that taxes and shares the gains.
I'd say **motorway trunk runs** will be automated first.
think: My exact job is **first in line** when robots come in 2031.
With **two weeks of savings**, I can't quit to retrain full-time.
do: Double up on **electrics study** to two evenings a week.
Apply to maintain the **driverless trucks** at the hub.
Ask for a **transfer to days** so study fits around work.
S2.quote: Hub to hub, motorway, at night, no customers. My exact job is the first in line once the robots come in 2031.
fieldNote: Bilal is clear-eyed that **trunk runs** are the most automatable driving there is.
He treats the **three-year gap** as a countdown for study.
His **excitement** about the tech sits alongside real fear of losing his income.

steps.text: Study electrics two evenings a week instead of one
Apply to the hub's driverless truck maintenance team
Back union demands for a funded retraining queue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this right if the government starts on day one. I'd write to our local politician and post about it. People like me need paid evening courses, not leaflets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years plus three for robots means about 2034 before trunk runs really go. I'd be qualified as an electrician by then if I keep going. The risk is that there are loads of us retraining at once and not that many jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the electrical qualification within three years and get my first site experience at weekends. I'd save the overtime from Christmas peak each year. And I'd keep my artic licence current, just in case driving lasts longer than they say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in control. It's a race, but I think I can win it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you get weekend site experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate's dad, Tony, runs a small electrical firm doing house rewires. He's said before I can come carry cable and learn. I'd take him up on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your housemates who drive too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start something now, anything. Kyle drives vans and thinks the robots won't bother with vans. Maybe he's right, but I'd rather he had a backup.

say: I'd say five years works if the government starts on **day one**.
I'd write to our **local politician** asking for paid evening courses.
think: Trunk runs really go around **2034**, by which time I could be qualified.
The risk is **too many people** retraining at once for too few jobs.
do: Finish the **electrical qualification** within three years.
Gain weekend **site experience** with a friend's dad's firm.
Save the **Christmas peak** overtime each year.
feel: **Anxious** but **in control**, like a race he can win.
S3.quote: Five years plus three for robots means about 2034 before trunk runs really go. I'd be qualified as an electrician by then if I keep going.
fieldNote: Bilal sees the main danger as **crowding**: everyone retraining at once.
He keeps his **artic licence** as a hedge, which shows caution under the confidence.
He'd still lose his **driving income**, so he stays anxious despite a plan.

steps.text: Finish the evening electrical qualification within three years
Save the Christmas peak overtime each year
Write to the local politician asking for paid evening courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to build a fair system, with drivers trained and the gains shared. I'd still push the same message, but calmer. No point screaming when there's time to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving would just be my twenties. With robots around 2039, I'd have more than enough time to become an electrician and maybe run my own small firm. I'd still worry about mates who don't plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrics course at a normal pace, finish in four years, then switch jobs around thirty-two. Before that, I'd keep driving nights for the extra pay. I'd also try using AI to find cheap, decent training and help mates do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for other people. For me it feels like a fair amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to help those mates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up a little group chat for drivers who want to retrain, share courses, share what AI tools actually work. It costs nothing. Half of them won't join, but some will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside to having ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People relax. The union might think it's got forever, and then suddenly it's 2036 and nothing's been agreed. I'd be the annoying one bringing it up every meeting.

say: I'd say a **decade** is time to build a fair system.
I'd push the same message, **calmer**, organising instead of shouting.
think: Robots around **2039** give me time to become an **electrician**.
Driving would just be my **twenties**, but mates who don't plan worry me.
do: Finish the electrics course in **four years** and switch around thirty-two.
Keep driving **nights** for the extra pay meanwhile.
Start a **group chat** to help drivers find training.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for other people, while feeling there's **enough time**.
S4.quote: Driving would just be my twenties. With robots around 2039, I'd have more than enough time to become an electrician and maybe run my own small firm.
fieldNote: Ten years makes Bilal's worry mostly about **other drivers**, not himself.
He fears the **union relaxing** more than the technology.
He'd use AI to help colleagues find **training**, a typically outward move.

steps.text: Finish the electrical course over four years and switch jobs
Keep driving nights for the higher pay until qualified
Start a group chat helping drivers share training courses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because trunk runs go first and I'd be halfway through a course. What would help is paid evening study, so I'm not choosing between rent and a qualification. And a union with a seat at the table when the carrier buys the driverless trucks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about sleep. Night drivers are knackered all the time, and you can't retrain properly when you're running on four hours. Getting drivers onto days while they study would help as much as money.

headlineQuote: Night drivers are knackered all the time, and you can't retrain properly when you're running on four hours.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** night trunk driver for a parcel carrier, with two weeks of savings.
He shares a house with friends and uses **AI every day**, including to study electrics.
He loves the technology but insists **unions** must secure workers' share of the gains.
He knows **motorway trunk runs** are first to be automated and treats the robot gap as a countdown.
Longer timelines turn his worry towards **other drivers** who won't plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because trunk runs go first while he's **mid-course**.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid evening study** and day shifts so he can retrain without losing rent money.
